OMMA registration remains optional; OBNDD's mandatory directive applies only to manufacturers and distributors, not dispensaries. tracks.detail: The dedicated DEA application forms for Medical Marijuana Manufacturer, Bulk Manufacturer (cultivator/grower), Analytical Lab, and Distributor did NOT launch before the 60-day window closed. 60-DAY WINDOW NOW CLOSED (JUNE 29): The effective final day was June 29, 2026 — the Saturday-rule shift of the 60th calendar day (June 27), confirmed by Manatt, Phelps & Phillips. This was NOT a formal DEA extension; it was the standard federal procedural rule. Operators who filed Form 225 with medical-marijuana drug codes 7362/7353/7386 by June 29 hold safe-harbor operating authority during DEA's six-month review. Operators who did not file missed the expedited window — may still apply at deadiversion.usdoj.gov outside the window but without safe-harbor protection during review. Fees under Form 225: $3,699/yr (Manufacturer), $1,850/yr (Distributor), $296/yr (Analytical Lab). DEA has confirmed that operators who apply via Form 225 before the dedicated portal launches do NOT need to reapply. OBNDD (May 8, 2026) states manufacturers and distributors are REQUIRED to obtain DEA registration; enforcement grace period runs to January 1, 2027.

items.headline: Georgia Proposes Allowing USPS and Private-Carrier Delivery of Medical Cannabis — First State to Test Schedule III Mail-Delivery Interpretation
items.summary: Georgia's Access to Medical Cannabis Commission formally posted proposed rules on August 13, 2026 allowing medical cannabis to be delivered directly to patients via the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) and private carriers such as FedEx and UPS. The commission's legal rationale is that the April 28, 2026 Schedule III rescheduling order removed medical cannabis from the CSA provisions that prohibit mailing Schedule I and II controlled substances. Under the proposal, shipments would be restricted to the Georgia address associated with a registered patient's medical cannabis card — it covers only intrastate Georgia-to-Georgia delivery, not interstate commerce. A public hearing on the proposed rules is scheduled for September 16, 2026 in Atlanta. This makes Georgia the first state to formally test the mail-delivery implications of the Trump administration's Schedule III rescheduling order through a state regulatory proposal.
items.whyItMatters: For CAKE and its Oklahoma wholesale dispensary customers, the Georgia proposal is a signal — not an action item. It represents the first state regulatory body formally testing whether Schedule III status removes the federal mail-prohibition that made mailing cannabis a federal crime under Schedule I/II. If confirmed, the same legal theory could eventually support similar proposals in Oklahoma, enabling new dispensary-to-patient delivery models. However, several layers of uncertainty remain: USPS has not confirmed it will accept cannabis shipments even under Schedule III; private carriers (FedEx, UPS) have their own compliance policies; OMMA has issued no comparable Oklahoma rule; and the underlying legal interpretation could be challenged by DOJ or USPS. Oklahoma operators should treat this as an early indicator of where Schedule III rescheduling implications may lead — not as authorization to begin cannabis mail shipments. The proposed rules also create a discourse risk: the Georgia story is likely to circulate with operators claiming mail delivery is now generally permitted, when in reality it is limited to a proposed Georgia rule that has not yet taken effect and has not been validated by USPS or federal authorities.

items.headline: Texas Senate Race Polls as Statistical Tie — Delta-8 Hemp Ban Becomes Major Campaign Wedge; Talarico Calls It 'Gift to the Cartels,' Accuses Paxton of Protecting Alcohol/Tobacco Donors
items.summary: Democratic Texas U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico is using the state's delta-8 hemp ban (effective July 31, 2026) as a central campaign issue against Republican nominee and state Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico called the ban 'a gift to the cartels,' said Texas is 'going back to the days of prohibition,' and alleged that Paxton supports cannabis prohibition 'to enrich the big beer and big tobacco lobby' donating to his campaign. Paxton previously sued Texas municipalities for decriminalizing marijuana and has taken a consistent anti-cannabis enforcement position as state AG. The race is a statistical tie: a Fox News poll (July 23–27) showed Talarico up 3 points (51%–48%); a Texas Public Opinion Research poll (July 15–17) showed Talarico up 5 points (45%–40%); and a University of Texas poll showed Paxton up 1 point (43%–42%). The Texas Senate race was featured as the lead story in the Marijuana Moment August 17, 2026 newsletter under the headline 'Senate candidates clash on cannabis.'
items.whyItMatters: For CAKE and its Oklahoma wholesale dispensary customers, the Texas Senate race has two layers of direct relevance. First, Texas is Oklahoma's largest neighboring market — the Texas delta-8 hemp ban (July 31) has already forced up to 13,000 Texas businesses to exit the hemp-derived THC market, and the political consequences of that enforcement are now playing out in a competitive Senate race. This previews the political environment that will greet the House when it returns August 31 to consider the Senate CR's hemp delay provision: the Texas race shows that hemp enforcement is genuinely electorally consequential in Republican-leaning states, creating pressure on House Republicans from both hemp-friendly and hemp-ban constituencies. Second, the Texas Senate seat outcome will directly affect the Senate balance of power and thus the post-midterm legislative path for a permanent hemp regulatory fix, SAFER Banking Act passage, and broader cannabis reform after the ALJ process resolves. A Talarico win would narrow or eliminate the Republican Senate margin; a Paxton win (or a broader Republican Senate expansion) would deepen resistance to cannabis-friendly legislation. The race's statistical tie at this stage makes it a genuine November variable, not a safe Republican hold.

items.summary: Marijuana reform has emerged as a significant issue in the 2026 midterm elections on both sides of the aisle, according to an August 15, 2026 CNBC analysis. Josh Shapiro (pro-recreational legalization) against Republican Stacy Garrity (anti-legalization). The Texas governor's race involves hemp-derived THC products policy: Gov. Greg Abbott has called for tighter regulation rather than an outright ban, while opposing adult-use legalization. NORML political director Morgan Fox described cannabis as 'a very popular issue among voters.' More than 20 GOP senators and several House members have signed letters urging the White House to halt federal rescheduling, illustrating significant Republican congressional resistance at the federal level despite broad public polling support.
items.whyItMatters: For CAKE and its Oklahoma wholesale dispensary customers, the November 2026 midterm elections are the most significant near-term political variable for federal cannabis legislation beyond the current administrative and judicial tracks. The current Republican-led Congress has been resistant to SAFER Banking Act passage, a permanent legislative hemp regulatory fix, and broader cannabis access legislation. If Democrats make significant gains in November, the legislative path for cannabis-friendly bills reopens; if Republicans expand their majority, administrative rescheduling via the April 28 order remains the practical ceiling. Specifically at stake post-midterms: any permanent legislative resolution of the November 12 hemp ban (the Senate CR provides only a 29-day delay and is not yet law), the long-term fate of SAFER Banking for cannabis financial access, and any broader descheduling legislation. The ALJ recommended decision (expected months after the August 17 brief deadline) will land in a post-midterm political environment that may or may not be receptive to formalizing Schedule III.

source.name: CNBC — Marijuana reform is emerging as a midterm elections issue on both sides of the aisle (August 15, 2026)

items.headline: Senate Confirms Todd Blanche as Permanent Attorney General 50-49 — Reduces Legal Risk to April 28 Rescheduling Order
items.summary: The U.S. Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as permanent Attorney General on August 8, 2026 by a 50-49 vote. All Democratic senators voted against confirmation, joined by Republican Sens. Susan Collins (ME) and Lisa Murkowski (AK). Blanche secured final confirmation after the Senate Judiciary Committee advanced his nomination 12-10 on August 4 — Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis provided the decisive committee votes after securing an agreement clarifying the scope of President Trump's IRS immunity deal and rescinding the administration's $1.8 billion 'Anti-Weaponization Fund.' Blanche overcame a final floor obstacle after securing the vote of Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA). His nomination had been complicated by questions over the Epstein files, the Trump IRS settlement, and pardon oversight — all unrelated to cannabis regulation.
items.whyItMatters: Blanche's confirmation as permanent AG materially reduces the 'Acting AG signing authority' legal risk narrative for the April 28, 2026 Schedule III rescheduling order. Legal analysts (Lexology, National Law Review) note that a permanent AG is exceedingly unlikely to unwind an order he personally issued. The D.C. Circuit stay motion in Cases 26-1106/1130/1136 is NOT resolved by Blanche's confirmation — the court's APA and CSA review is independent of whether the signing official was Acting AG or permanent AG at the time of signing, and the stay motion remains fully briefed and can be decided at any time. The discourse entry 'watch-blanche-confirmation-uncertainty-april28-order' warned about this risk; it is now resolved in the affirmative. Oklahoma OBNDD registration obligations and the January 1, 2027 enforcement grace period are unchanged. The adult-use broader-rescheduling ALJ proceeding (post-hearing briefs due August 17, 2026) is unaffected by Blanche's confirmation status.

source.name: NPR — Senate votes to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general (August 8, 2026)

secondarySource.name: Washington Post — Senate narrowly approves Todd Blanche as AG, capping tough confirmation fight (August 8, 2026)

items.headline: DEA Files Federal Court Brief Defending HHC Schedule I Classification — Signals Enforcement Posture on Synthetic Cannabinoids Ahead of November 12 Hemp Ban
items.summary: The Drug Enforcement Administration filed a federal court brief on or around August 14, 2026 defending its position that hexahydrocannabinol (HHC) is an illegal Schedule I synthetic cannabinoid — not legal hemp — in response to lawsuits by two hemp companies challenging DEA's May 4, 2026 final rule giving HHC its own Schedule I drug code. DEA's May 4 rule explicitly classified chemically converted tetrahydrocannabinols (including HHC derived from hemp feedstocks) as Schedule I substances regardless of their hemp origin, citing that they fall within the 'tetrahydrocannabinols' scheduling category and that hemp-derived synthetic conversion does not qualify for the hemp exemption. Two hemp companies filed separate legal challenges; the August brief is DEA's defense of its position in that ongoing litigation.
items.whyItMatters: DEA's active federal court defense of HHC's Schedule I status confirms its enforcement posture on synthetic and chemically converted cannabinoids: hemp-derived origin does not exempt a compound from Schedule I scheduling if it is a THC analog or synthetic equivalent. This directly reinforces the November 12, 2026 hemp ban context: the Senate CR's hemp delay provision explicitly carves out synthetic cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. — fully consistent with DEA's litigated position. Oklahoma operators selling HHC, THC-O acetate, or similar converted products face Schedule I recriminalization on November 12 regardless of any hemp CR outcome. This filing does not affect OMMA-licensed cannabis cultivators and processors operating under the April 28 Schedule III order — it is scoped to synthetic hemp-derived compounds, not state-licensed medical marijuana.

source.name: Marijuana Moment — DEA Says Hemp Company Can't Challenge Agency's Stance That Synthetic Cannabis Compound HHC Is Federally Banned (August 2026)

items.headline: Glass House Brands Q2 2026 Earnings — +34% Revenue Growth; CEO Cites Interstate Commerce Infrastructure Positioning
items.summary: Glass House Brands (NYSE: GLASF) reported Q2 2026 financial results on August 13, 2026, posting approximately 34% revenue growth year-over-year. CEO Kyle Kazan's prepared remarks described the company's large-scale California cultivation infrastructure as 'foundational' positioning for anticipated authorized federal interstate cannabis commerce — marking one of the first major multistate operators to explicitly describe a post-Schedule III interstate commerce build-out strategy on an earnings call. Glass House, which listed on the NYSE June 30, 2026 as the second U.S. cannabis company on a major exchange, also retained former senior DEA official Matt Murphy in July 2026 to advise on federal regulatory strategy.
items.whyItMatters: Glass House's interstate commerce framing signals that well-capitalized multistate operators are positioning for the next anticipated regulatory milestone — authorized federal interstate cannabis commerce — using Schedule III and the April 28 order as the regulatory foundation. For CAKE, operating exclusively in Oklahoma's intrastate wholesale market, this is a structural signal: if and when interstate commerce is authorized, large-scale operators with existing DEA registration, NYSE listings, and cross-state cultivation infrastructure will have significant structural advantages. The immediate compliance takeaway: Glass House's earnings remarks do NOT signal that interstate commerce is currently permitted (it is not); they signal that large operators are building infrastructure for what they expect will eventually be authorized. The April 28 Schedule III order is the foundation Glass House is positioning on — Oklahoma operators who have not filed DEA Form 225 are further behind that structural curve.

source.name: Glass House Brands — Q2 2026 Earnings (August 13, 2026)

items.headline: Trulieve Completes Corporate Redomicile from British Columbia to Delaware — First NYSE-Listed Cannabis Company Now U.S.-Domiciled; Direct Consequence of Schedule III
items.summary: On August 11, 2026, Trulieve Cannabis Corp. (NYSE: TRLV) completed its corporate redomicile from British Columbia, Canada to Delaware, becoming the first U.S. cannabis company on the NYSE to be U.S.-domiciled. Shareholders approved the move 99.5% on August 5; the British Columbia Supreme Court issued its final order August 10; and domestication was filed with Delaware on August 11. CEO Kim Rivers stated the redomicile 'expands access to U.S. investors and enhancing eligibility for broader index inclusion.' This follows Trulieve's NYSE debut on June 10, 2026 — the first U.S. plant-touching cannabis company to list on a major U.S. exchange.
items.whyItMatters: The Delaware redomicile is a direct structural consequence of Schedule III rescheduling. Without the April 28 order enabling the NYSE listing, the Canadian domicile provided advantages for OTC trading. Schedule III's removal of the NYSE barrier (June 10) enabled the listing, and U.S. domiciliation now unlocks expanded access to U.S. institutional investors and potential inclusion in broad stock market indices requiring U.S.-incorporated companies. This demonstrates that Schedule III is catalyzing fundamental corporate restructuring — not just regulatory relabeling. For CAKE and its Oklahoma wholesale dispensary customers, this signals accelerating institutional capital concentration among large multistate operators, which may continue to exert downward pressure on the wholesale pricing environment that CAKE operates in.

source.name: Trulieve — Trulieve Completes Redomicile from British Columbia to Delaware (August 11, 2026)

secondarySource.name: PR Newswire — Trulieve Completes Redomicile from British Columbia to Delaware

items.headline: Square Ends Hemp/CBD Payment Processing Ahead of November Federal Ban — Merchant Deadline October 15, Account Closures November 5
items.summary: Square, a widely-used point-of-sale and payment processing platform, announced it will no longer allow businesses to sell CBD and hemp-derived products on its platform in light of the upcoming November 12, 2026 federal hemp THC ban. Merchants with mixed catalogs must remove hemp and CBD items by October 15, 2026; merchants whose catalogs are primarily hemp-focused will have their Square accounts closed November 5, 2026. The move makes Square the first major payment processor to announce proactive enforcement of the federal hemp deadline.
items.whyItMatters: For Oklahoma dispensaries or hemp retailers that use Square for hemp-derived product sales (CBD gummies, hemp beverages, THCA flower, delta-8 products), the operative deadline is now October 15, 2026 — a full month before the federal statutory date of November 12. Critically, Square's November 5 account-closure date falls before the Senate CR's proposed December 11 delay, meaning even if Congress passes a hemp ban delay, Square's private enforcement schedule will not be reversed by that legislation. Operators relying on Square for any hemp-adjacent product category should begin transitioning payment processing and catalog management immediately, without waiting for legislative resolution.

source.name: Marijuana Moment — Square Tells Businesses To Stop Selling Hemp And CBD Products

items.headline: House Returns August 31 — Senate CR Hemp Delay (Nov 12 → Dec 11) NOT Yet Law; November 12 Remains Operative Deadline
items.summary: The Senate passed its continuing resolution 90-6 on August 8, 2026, including a provision to delay the federal hemp THC ban from November 12 to December 11, 2026 (with an immediate November 12 carve-out for synthetic cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L., such as HHC and THC-O acetate). The House is in recess until August 31. The House version of the CR (passed July 2026) runs through December 4 and contains no hemp delay provision. The two chambers must reconcile their versions before any delay takes effect; Senate leaders Budd and Ricketts have indicated they will press the House to reject or strip the hemp delay when Congress returns.
items.whyItMatters: November 12, 2026 remains the operative compliance planning deadline for all Oklahoma hemp operators and any OMMA licensees that sell hemp-derived products. The Senate CR has NOT become law. When the House returns August 31, it could pass the Senate version as-is (delay to December 11), pass its own version without a delay (November 12 stands), or fail to reach agreement (triggering a government shutdown with no effect on the statutory hemp ban date). Even if a delay is ultimately enacted, synthetic cannabinoids (HHC, THC-O acetate, THC-B, etc.) face November 12 recriminalization under the Senate CR's own carve-out language. Oklahoma operators should not pause November 12 compliance preparations based on Senate action alone.

source.name: Agri-Pulse — Senate passes bill to avert shutdown, delay hemp ban as midterms loom

items.headline: Senate Agriculture Committee Farm Bill 2.0 Fails 10-11 Committee Vote on August 7 — Dead Before August Recess; September Markup Next Possible Window
items.summary: The Senate Agriculture Committee failed to advance the Agricultural Act of 2026 (Farm Bill 2.0) out of committee by a 10-11 vote on August 7, 2026, the day after the August 6 markup session opened. The primary barrier was a SNAP cost-share dispute: Republicans proposed a one-year delay on new state cost-sharing requirements for SNAP, while Democrats sought a two-year delay and opposed language exempting high-error-rate states. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) voted by proxy; Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-AL) left the room before the final vote — even with Tuberville present the tally would have been 11-11 (still a failure). Chairman Boozman placed the markup in recess; a second vote is expected in September 2026 when the Senate returns from its August recess.
items.whyItMatters: For Oklahoma OMMA-licensed operators, this confirms the Farm Bill is NOT a vehicle for any hemp THC delay before September 2026. The Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (Senate-passed CR, containing a November 12 → December 11 hemp delay for most products) remains the ONLY near-term mechanism — and it is still not enacted law, as the House must act and is not expected back until September. A hemp delay amendment could theoretically be added to the Farm Bill on the Senate floor when markup reopens in September, but compressed timelines (Senate floor passage, House-Senate conference, presidential signature before November 12) make enactment via that path extremely unlikely before November 12. CAKE and its wholesale dispensary accounts must maintain full November 12 hemp compliance posture for hemp-derived THCA-flower, delta-8, delta-10, and high-potency hemp beverages. The November 12, 2026 federal hemp redefinition (Section 781 of P.L. 119-37) is legally unchanged.

source.name: American Ag Network — Senate Ag Committee Fails to Advance Farm Bill Over SNAP Dispute (August 7, 2026)

items.headline: Senate Tables Budd Amendment 61-32; Full CR Passes 90-6 — Hemp Delay (Nov 12 → Dec 11) Survives Senate; Heads to House; NOT Yet Law
items.summary: On August 8, 2026, the Senate voted 61-32 to table (procedurally defeat) Sen. Ted Budd’s (R-NC) amendment to strip the hemp THC product ban delay from the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (CR). The underlying CR then passed the full Senate 90-6. The Senate-passed CR delays most federal hemp restrictions from November 12 to December 11, 2026 — a 29-day extension. Critically, synthetic cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. (including HHC, THC-O acetate, and similar compounds) are NOT covered by the delay and remain recriminalized November 12 as originally scheduled. The CR now moves to the House of Representatives, which is in recess until approximately the first week of September 2026 and passed its own competing CR in July with NO hemp delay provision. Both chambers must pass matching legislation and the President must sign it before any hemp delay becomes law.
items.whyItMatters: The Senate’s 90-6 passage is an important but incomplete step — the hemp delay is still NOT enacted law. Oklahoma operators should NOT treat Senate passage as confirmation of a December 11 deadline. The House CR contains no hemp delay, the House is not in session until September, and the 35-AG coalition and Sens. Budd and Ricketts have explicitly committed to pressing the House to reject the delay in conference. CAKE and its wholesale dispensary accounts must maintain full November 12 compliance posture for hemp-derived products (THCA-flower, delta-8, delta-10, hemp beverages exceeding 0.3% total THC or 0.4mg THC per container). Even if the delay is ultimately enacted, it provides only 29 additional days (to December 11) and does not protect synthetic cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. The January 1, 2027 OBNDD enforcement grace period for DEA registration remains unchanged.

source.name: The Hill — Senate tables hemp amendment at center of funding fight, allowing one-month delay of ban (August 8, 2026)

secondarySource.name: Roll Call — Funding patch passes Senate to head off fall shutdown (August 8, 2026)

items.headline: Senate Parliamentarian Rules Budd Amendment to Strip Hemp Delay Is Germane — 50-Vote Threshold Applies; Vote Possible August 9; 13 Bipartisan Cosponsors Including First Democrat
items.summary: The Senate Parliamentarian has ruled that Sen. Ted Budd's (R-NC) amendment to remove the 30-day hemp THC product ban delay from the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (CR) is germane to the underlying legislation, clearing it to pass with a simple 50-vote majority rather than the 60-vote filibuster threshold. The amendment has grown to 13 bipartisan cosponsors — including Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), the first Democrat to join — signaling broad congressional support for keeping the November 12 hemp ban on schedule despite White House lobbying for the delay. A vote on the Budd amendment could occur as soon as August 9, 2026. If the amendment passes, the Senate CR would no longer include any hemp delay provision, effectively reinstating November 12 as the operative deadline before the bill reaches the House — eliminating the need for House-Senate reconciliation on the hemp provision.
items.whyItMatters: This is the single most significant development for Oklahoma hemp-adjacent operators since the Senate passed the CR with the delay. The Parliamentarian ruling dramatically increases the probability that November 12, 2026 remains the operative federal hemp compliance deadline — hemp-derived THCA-flower, delta-8, delta-10, and high-potency hemp beverages face recriminalization on that date with no further delay. Oklahoma dispensaries carrying these products and CAKE's wholesale accounts serving them must treat November 12 as a hard deadline. Even if Budd's amendment fails in the Senate, the House CR contains no hemp delay provision and House action is not expected until September — November 12 remains the primary planning assumption in either scenario. Synthetic cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. (HHC, THC-O acetate) face recriminalization November 12 regardless of any legislative outcome.

source.name: The Marijuana Herald — Senate Parliamentarian Rules Amendment to Strip Hemp THC Ban Delay Can Pass With 50 Votes

secondarySource.name: MJBizDaily — Democratic Senator Backs GOP-Led Effort to Keep Hemp THC Ban Alive (August 6, 2026)

items.headline: White House Actively Lobbying for CR Hemp Delay as of August 6 — Not Yet Enacted, House Must Still Act
items.summary: The Marijuana Moment August 6, 2026 daily newsletter confirms the White House is actively pushing Congress to preserve the 30-day hemp THC product ban delay (November 12 → December 11, 2026) in the federal continuing resolution. The Senate passed the CR with the delay provision intact; Sen. Ted Budd's amendment to strip it did not prevail. The House passed a competing CR through December 4 with no hemp language; the House is not expected to act until September. The White House lobbying signal indicates executive branch preference for the delay but is not enactment.
items.whyItMatters: White House support modestly increases the probability the House eventually adopts the Senate version, but three steps remain: House floor vote on the Senate text, bicameral reconciliation, and presidential signature — all expected no earlier than September. Oklahoma operators should not treat this as permission to slow-roll November 12 compliance preparations. Even if enacted, the CR delay provides only 30 additional days (to December 11) and does NOT delay the ban on synthetic cannabinoids not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. (e.g., HHC, THC-O acetate). Cultivators and manufacturers with hemp-adjacent product lines must plan for November 12 unless a signed law explicitly changes it.

items.headline: Senate Farm Bill August 6 Markup Confirms No Hemp Provisions — CR Remains Only Active Delay Vehicle
items.summary: Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman convened the scheduled August 6 markup of the Agricultural Act of 2026 (Farm Bill 2.0), and the committee's baseline draft deliberately excluded all hemp THC provisions. A committee aide confirmed hemp amendments would have precluded Senate floor advancement under the 60-vote threshold. The markup focused on E15 year-round fuel access and SNAP administration provisions. No hemp-ban delay, modification, or standalone hemp language was included in or offered to the committee's baseline text.
items.whyItMatters: For Oklahoma cultivators, manufacturers, and dispensaries: this confirms the Senate Farm Bill is NOT the vehicle for any hemp THC ban delay or modification. The Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (Senate-passed CR with November 12 → December 11 delay) is the ONLY near-term mechanism — and it is not yet law, as the House passed a competing CR with no hemp language. CAKE and its retail customers should continue planning for the November 12, 2026 federal hemp definition change (0.3% total THC threshold, 0.4mg THC per container limit) unless and until the House passes the Senate CR version and the President signs it.

items.headline: 35 State/Territory AGs Send Bipartisan Letter Urging Congress to Let November 12 Hemp Ban Take Effect — Directed to House Speaker Johnson and Senate Majority Leader Thune
items.summary: On August 4, 2026, a bipartisan coalition of 35 state and territory attorneys general — led by Indiana AG Todd Rokita — sent a letter to U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune urging them to reject any legislative effort that would delay the November 12, 2026 implementation of the federal hemp THC product ban (Section 781 of P.L. 119-37). The letter warned that a delay would give the intoxicating hemp industry another opportunity to exploit a loophole that 'was already voted closed' and allow continued sales of unregulated products mimicking marijuana. California AG Rob Bonta issued a public press release joining the bipartisan coalition. The letter was sent the same day the Senate was advancing the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (CR) — which includes a provision delaying most hemp restrictions from November 12 to December 11 for most products. Reported by Law360, Cannabis Business Times, Washington Examiner, and the Indiana Lawyer.
items.whyItMatters: For Oklahoma OMMA-licensed dispensaries and cultivators, the 35-AG letter adds substantial political pressure on the House to reject or strip the Senate's hemp delay provision when it returns from recess in September. The House passed its own CR in July through December 4 with NO hemp delay provision — the House's default position aligns with the AGs' position. This significantly narrows the path to an enacted hemp delay before November 12, 2026. Oklahoma dispensaries carrying hemp-derived THCA-flower, delta-8, delta-10, or hemp beverages should maintain full November 12 compliance posture regardless of the Senate's CR passage. The November 12, 2026 federal hemp ban (Section 781 of P.L. 119-37) is legally unchanged.

source.name: Cannabis Business Times — 35 Attorneys General Tell Congress to Keep Hemp THC Ban Put (August 4, 2026)

secondarySource.name: Law360 — 35 AGs Urge Congress Not To Delay Hemp Ban Rollout (August 4, 2026)

items.headline: Senate Passes CR (Final Vote ~August 4) With Hemp Delay November 12 → December 11 for Most Products — Synthetics Still Banned November 12; House Must Still Act; NOT Yet Law
items.summary: Following the 89-4 procedural cloture vote on August 3, 2026, the U.S. Senate passed the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (CR) on approximately August 4, 2026, confirming government funding through December 11 and including a provision delaying most federal hemp restrictions from November 12, 2026 to December 11, 2026. Multiple secondary outlets — including HotAir ('Stopgap Spending Bill Passes Senate To Avoid Shutdown'), BevNET ('Senate Approves 30-Day Hemp Deadline Extension'), and Yahoo News ('Senate approves more than $180 billion in 2026 funding before August recess') — report Senate final passage. Sen. Ted Budd (R-NC) filed an amendment to strip the hemp delay from the CR; the amendment did not prevail. CRITICAL DISTINCTIONS: (1) Synthetic cannabinoids 'not capable of being naturally produced by a Cannabis sativa L. plant' are NOT covered by the delay and remain subject to recriminalization on November 12 as scheduled under the Senate CR text. (2) The Senate-passed CR is NOT yet enacted law — the House passed a competing CR through December 4 with NO hemp delay provision, and both chambers must reconcile before the President can sign. House action is not expected until September at the earliest.
items.whyItMatters: This is the furthest the hemp delay has advanced legislatively, but it is not enacted law and the November 12, 2026 federal hemp ban (Section 781 of P.L. 119-37) remains the operative legal standard. Oklahoma dispensaries carrying hemp-derived THCA-flower, delta-8, or delta-10, and CAKE's wholesale accounts serving such dispensaries, must maintain full November 12, 2026 compliance posture. Even if enacted, the delay is only 30 days (to December 11) and would not cover synthetic hemp derivatives. The 35-AG bipartisan letter sent August 4 (see: state-ags-35-letter-oppose-hemp-delay-aug4) adds significant political pressure on the House to reject or strip the delay in conference. Treat any enacted delay as a windfall only if and when signed by the President.

secondarySource.name: BevNET — Senate Approves 30-Day Hemp Deadline Extension (August 4, 2026)

items.headline: Senate Votes 89-4 on Cloture to Advance CR with Hemp Delay to December 11 (August 3, 2026) — Procedural Vote, NOT Final Passage; Final Floor Vote Still Pending; House Must Still Act; NOT Yet Law
items.summary: The U.S. Senate voted 89-4 on August 3, 2026 to invoke cloture — a procedural vote to end debate and advance the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (CR) toward a final floor vote. The CR, released by the Senate Appropriations Committee on August 2, includes a provision delaying most federal hemp restrictions (Section 781 of P.L. 119-37) from November 12, 2026 to December 11, 2026. Critically, the 89-4 cloture vote is NOT final Senate floor passage — a final vote is still pending. Additionally, the House passed its own CR in July through December 4 without any hemp delay provision; the two versions must be reconciled before any CR with a hemp delay can be sent to the President. House action is not expected until September at the earliest, after Congress returns from August recess. Synthetic cannabinoids 'that are not capable of being naturally produced by a Cannabis sativa L. plant' are excluded from the delay and would still be recriminalized November 12. Reported by the Washington Times and Forbes (August 3, 2026). BevNET and Brewbound headlines reading 'Senate Approves 30-Day Hemp Deadline Extension' refer to the procedural cloture advancement, not a final enacted law.
items.whyItMatters: The 89-4 cloture margin signals near-unanimous Senate support and makes it highly likely the Senate will pass the CR with the hemp delay in its final floor vote. However, this is NOT enacted law — the November 12, 2026 federal hemp ban (Section 781 of P.L. 119-37) remains in effect. Oklahoma dispensaries carrying hemp-derived THCA-flower, delta-8, delta-10, or hemp beverages, and cultivators sourcing out-of-state genetics, should maintain full November 12 compliance posture. If the Senate passes the CR in its final vote AND the House accepts the Senate's hemp language AND the President signs before November 12, the operative deadline would shift to December 11 for most products (synthetics excepted) — treat that as a windfall only when signed by the President. The House, which must accept or conference the Senate's hemp language, is not expected to act until September at the earliest.

source.name: Washington Times — Senate Advances Government Funding Stopgap (August 3, 2026)

secondarySource.name: Forbes — Senate Moves To Delay Federal Ban On Hemp THC Products (August 3, 2026)

items.headline: Senate Funding Bill (CR) Draft Includes Provision to Delay Most Federal Hemp Restrictions Until December 11, 2026 — Synthetics Still Recriminalized November 12; Not Yet Law
items.summary: Senate leaders released a continuing resolution (CR/spending bill) draft on August 2, 2026 that includes a provision delaying most federal hemp restrictions from November 12, 2026 until December 11, 2026. The CR would hold the Section 781 of P.L. 119-37 hemp redefinition — the 0.3% total-THC threshold, the 0.4 mg per final-product container cap, and related provisions — in abeyance for an additional 29 days for most products. Critically, synthetic cannabinoids 'that are not capable of being naturally produced by a Cannabis sativa L. plant' would NOT receive the delay and would still be recriminalized on November 12 as scheduled. Reported by Marijuana Herald and Marijuana Moment on August 2, 2026, with Senate vote expected during the week of August 3–8. This delay provision is NOT in the Farm Bill (Senate Ag Committee markup scheduled August 6) — it is in a separate legislative vehicle, the FY2026 Continuing Resolution. The House passed a clean CR without any hemp delay language; the House would need to separately act in September to extend the delay further.
items.whyItMatters: For Oklahoma dispensaries carrying hemp-derived THCA-flower, delta-8, or delta-10 products, and cultivators sourcing out-of-state hemp genetics, this development is meaningful but is NOT a reason to pause compliance planning. The Senate CR is not yet law — it must pass the full Senate floor vote and then the House must act separately. Even if enacted, the delay is only 29 days (to December 11), and synthetics not naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L. are still recriminalized November 12 with no delay. The Farm Bill track (August 6 markup) does NOT contain a hemp delay provision. Plan for November 12 compliance as the controlling operative date; treat any enacted delay as a windfall only if and when signed by the President.

items.headline: Hemp Safety Enforcement Act (Paul/Klobuchar/Ernst) — State Opt-Out Approach to November 12 Federal Hemp Ban; Distinct From Lawful Hemp Protection Act
items.summary: The Hemp Safety Enforcement Act was introduced in the Senate on April 16, 2026, with Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY) as lead sponsor, joined by Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) and Sen. Joni Ernst (R-IA). The bill (companion to H.R. 7010 in the House) takes a state opt-out approach to the November 12, 2026 federal hemp redefinition: rather than delaying or replacing the federal THC threshold, it would allow individual states to opt out of federal hemp enforcement within their borders — permitting state-regulated hemp markets to continue under state authority even after Section 781 of P.L. 119-37 takes effect. This approach is conceptually distinct from the Lawful Hemp Protection Act (Barr/Craig, introduced July 22, 2026), which would replace the federal definition with a new regulatory framework. The Hemp Safety Enforcement Act has not received a Senate committee hearing; no markup is scheduled; and the bill does not affect the November 12, 2026 federal hemp redefinition effective date as of August 2, 2026.
items.whyItMatters: For Oklahoma OMMA-licensed dispensaries and the CAKE wholesale network, the opt-out mechanism — if enacted — would mean Oklahoma could potentially continue state-regulated hemp sales even after the November 12 federal threshold takes effect. However, the bill has not passed any committee, has no markup scheduled, and faces significant floor obstacles. The November 12, 2026 federal hemp redefinition (Section 781 of P.L. 119-37) is legally unchanged as of August 2, 2026. Do not reduce November 12 compliance preparations based on this bill's existence. The presence of this distinct legislative vehicle (opt-out vs. delay vs. replacement) illustrates Congress's fragmented approach — no single bill has majority support, and the odds of any legislative fix before November 12 remain extremely low. Treat any enacted statutory change as a windfall only if and when signed by the President.

source.name: Sen. Rand Paul — Hemp Safety Enforcement Act (April 16, 2026)

Some operators are exploring in-state clones and tissue culture as alternatives with a potentially different risk profile under the new statutory language.
items.whyItMatters: Oklahoma cannabis cultivators who source genetics from out-of-state seed banks would lose access to interstate seed shipments after November 12, 2026 — unless the Lawful Hemp Protection Act or another bill passes. This is a distinct compliance risk from the hemp-derived product ban. Oklahoma cultivators should audit their genetics supply chain now: any seed shipments from other states after November 12 could expose the recipient and sender to federal charges. Establishing in-state tissue culture or clone sources before the deadline is the safest path if Congress does not act.

items.headline: Alabama ADPH Hearing on State Rescheduling Concluded July 22 — Decision Expected After August 5 Written Comment Deadline
items.summary: The Alabama Department of Public Health held the scheduled July 22 public hearing on whether to adopt the federal Schedule III rescheduling of marijuana under state law. Testimony was received from members of the public and government agencies. Conservative activists registered objections; only one speaker supported aligning with the federal change. Written public comments are accepted through August 5, 2026, after which ADPH must make its decision. Alabama's state health officer indicated the state 'fully intends' to follow the federal change but needs to work out implementation details.
items.whyItMatters: This confirms that federal Schedule III rescheduling does not automatically update state drug schedules — each state must take its own action. Alabama illustrates a state pushback process that delays automatic adoption. Oklahoma does not have a similar formal objection mechanism; OMMA has been monitoring the federal change and has issued guidance that 280E relief applies to Oklahoma operators regardless of DEA registration status. This Alabama proceeding is national context and does not directly affect Oklahoma OMMA operations.

items.headline: CONFIRMED: DEA 60-Day Window Extends to Monday June 29 — Saturday Rule; One Final Business Day for Form 225 Filers
items.summary: The 60th calendar day from the April 28 Federal Register publication falls on Saturday June 27. Standard federal rules shift the filing deadline to the next federal business day — Monday June 29, 2026. Manatt, Phelps & Phillips confirmed this: 'filings submitted on the next federal business day will be treated as timely.' This is NOT a formal DEA regulatory extension; it is the routine procedural rule that weekend deadlines roll to Monday. The dispensary-specific portal (mmapplication.diversion.dea.gov) closed June 22 and is unaffected. For cultivators, manufacturers, labs, and distributors: Monday June 29 is the effective last day to file DEA Form 225 (codes 7362/7353/7386) at deadiversion.usdoj.gov. Retain timestamped confirmation. Monday is also the first day of the broader-rescheduling ALJ hearing — file early morning.
items.whyItMatters: Oklahoma cultivators and processors who did not file Form 225 by Friday June 26 have one confirmed final opportunity — Monday June 29 — before the safe-harbor expedited window closes. OBNDD's mandatory registration directive (May 8, 2026) is unchanged; filing by June 29 preserves the right to continue operations during DEA's six-month review. Do not confuse this Saturday-rule extension with the circulating social media claim that 'DEA formally extended the 60-day window' — that rumor (a regulatory extension) remains false. The procedural extension to Monday is real, confirmed by law firms, and is available now.

items.headline: DEA Reschedules State Medical Marijuana & FDA-Approved Products to Schedule III
items.summary: Acting AG Todd Blanche issued a final order moving (1) marijuana in FDA-approved drug products and (2) marijuana under a qualifying state medical license from Schedule I to Schedule III, using treaty-implementation authority (21 U.S.C. 811(d)(1)) without traditional notice-and-comment. Recreational/adult-use, unlicensed marijuana, and synthetically derived THC remain Schedule I. A parallel expedited rulemaking on broader rescheduling was simultaneously initiated.
items.whyItMatters: Most consequential federal cannabis action in decades — creates new DEA registration duties, 280E tax relief, and treaty-compliance obligations for thousands of operators.

items.headline: DEA Registration Now Required — Expedited Window Closes ~June 26–27, 2026
items.summary: Dispensary portal opened April 29, 2026 at mmapplication.diversion.dea.gov ($794/yr, PayPal only) — OMMA states registration is OPTIONAL for dispensaries; the dedicated dispensary portal CLOSED June 22, 2026 per law firms Fennemore Craig and Foley Hoag LLP, 4 days before the 60-day Federal Register window closes June 26–27. Dedicated DEA application forms for Manufacturer, Bulk Manufacturer (cultivator/grower), Analytical Lab, and Distributor are NOT yet live as of 2026-06-22; a DEA Diversion Control notice (~May 11) said forms are 'coming in the coming weeks,' and the dedicated portal has not launched. The parallel pathway is DEA Form 225 with codes 7362/7353/7386 (fees: $3,699/yr manufacturer; $1,850/yr distributor; $296/yr lab). OBNDD states manufacturers and distributors are REQUIRED to register; enforcement grace period runs to January 1, 2027. The expedited 60-day window closes ~June 26–27 (60 days from April 28 Federal Register publication).
items.whyItMatters: Every cultivator, processor, lab, distributor, and dispensary faces a new federal registration layer. Dispensaries' dedicated portal CLOSED June 22 — dispensaries that missed must contact DEA directly at deadiversion.usdoj.gov before June 26–27. Manufacturers/cultivators must use Form 225 now with 2 days remaining as of June 24 — OBNDD says non-registration risks sanctions. Missing the expedited window means operating without safe-harbor during a six-month DEA review.

items.headline: OBNDD Mandates DEA Registration for OMMA Manufacturers & Distributors — Deadline ~June 27; Grace Period to Jan 1, 2027
items.summary: OBNDD Director Donnie Anderson directed that every OMMA registrant who is a "distributor or manufacturer" must obtain federal DEA registration. Applying within 60 days of the April 28 publication (~June 27, 2026) lets a business keep operating under state authority during DEA's six-month review. items.headline: Oklahoma Moratorium Extended to 2028 — HB 3143 Effective August 1; HB 3144 Cultivation Cap Confirmed at 2,550 Licenses
items.summary: AUGUST 2 UPDATE: HB 3144 is confirmed enacted — hard cap of 2,550 total commercial grower licenses statewide (authoritative figure confirmed August 2026; prior reporting cited 2,500). HB 3143 moratorium formally took effect August 1, 2026. Governor Kevin Stitt signed HB 3143 into law on May 7, 2026, extending Oklahoma's new-license moratorium from August 1, 2026 to August 1, 2028; the bill also prohibits transfer of any license currently under investigation. Companion HB 3144 — capping total cultivation licenses at 2,550 statewide — passed the House (82–15) and is confirmed enacted. The Oklahoma legislature adjourned sine die on May 14, 2026, closing the 2026 session. At House passage Oklahoma had 2,164 active grows, 686 processors, 1,421 dispensaries, and 58 transporters. The moratorium applies only to new licenses; existing licensees in good standing may still open new locations or transfer licenses with OMMA approval.
items.whyItMatters: The two-year moratorium extension is now law and formally in effect as of August 1, 2026 — no new cultivation or other cannabis licenses will be issued until at least August 2028. Existing grow licenses become scarcer and more valuable as transferable assets. HB 3144 is confirmed enacted — the 2,550-license cultivation cap locks the total count near its current level; new cultivation license applicants have no path until August 2028.

items.headline: Schedule III + Single Convention Activates Five New Compliance Burdens for Cultivators
items.summary: Because the rescheduling order is grounded in treaty-implementation authority, it increases — not reduces — cultivator compliance burdens: (1) SSNs for all personnel with controlled-substance access; (2) disclosure of upstream supplier DEA numbers; (3) DEA on-demand unscheduled inspection authority; (4) a crop purchase-and-resale mechanism where DEA serves as exclusive purchaser at a nominal price before crops can leave the facility; (5) parallel federal recordkeeping including quota reporting and import/export permits. The 2026 cultivator administrative fee is $113/kg on the 6,675 kg aggregate quota.
items.whyItMatters: Operators who assumed "rescheduling = deregulation" face a compliance shock; the DEA purchase-resale mechanism restructures the cultivation supply chain.

source.name: Cannabis Tech

items.headline: D.C. Circuit Cases 26-1106/1130/1136: SAM/NDASA Brief Filed June 4 — Nebraska/Indiana/Idaho Brief FILED June 26 (Marijuana Causes Psychiatric Harm; D'Souza to Testify) — Govt Response July 2; Louisiana Withdrew
items.summary: Three consolidated petition sets challenge the April 28 order: (1) Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM) + NDASA, filed May 4 — opening brief filed June 4; (2) AGs of Nebraska, Indiana, and Idaho, filed May 22 — opening brief CONFIRMED FILED June 26 per court deadline — states argue marijuana 'causes our citizens psychiatric harm and is linked to increases in homelessness, traffic accidents, illegal drug trafficking, and other crime'; states designated Dr. Deepak Cyril D'Souza (Yale Center for the Science of Cannabis) as expert witness on abuse liability; government (DOJ) response due July 2 (Louisiana initially co-filed but AG Liz Murrill sought dismissal May 29, leaving only Nebraska and Indiana as state-AG petitioners); (3) a coalition of five 'aggrieved persons' including addiction-treatment organizations (New Directions) and others, filed May 28. Arguments include: exceeds AG authority, violates APA notice-and-comment, implicates the major questions doctrine, and relies on a possibly unconstitutional ALJ structure. All petitioner groups seek both a stay and full vacatur. On June 9, NDASA + MMJ International Holdings + MMJ BioPharma Cultivation + MMJ BioPharma Labs separately filed a formal stay motion in Case 26-1136. No stay has been granted as of June 28, 2026.
items.whyItMatters: A stay could freeze the entire order — reverting state medical marijuana to Schedule I and nullifying registration, 280E relief, and research expansion. The Nebraska/Indiana brief (~June 26) and government response (July 2) are the next immediate court milestones; any subsequent stay ruling is the key risk event for Oklahoma operators.

items.headline: NDASA + MMJ BioPharma File D.C. Circuit Stay Motion — First Formal Stay Request in Case 26-1136
items.summary: On June 9, 2026, the National Drug and Alcohol Screening Association (NDASA), MMJ International Holdings, MMJ BioPharma Cultivation, and MMJ BioPharma Labs jointly filed a motion in D.C. Circuit Case No. 26-1136 seeking a stay of Attorney General Order No. 6754-2026 (the April 28 medical-marijuana rescheduling order). The petitioners argue (1) the order bypassed required notice-and-comment rulemaking; (2) the AG lacked authority to act without completing the statutory DEA hearing; and (3) MMJ International/MMJ BioPharma — which invested more than $10 million and nearly a decade developing cannabinoid pharmaceuticals through FDA/DEA channels — suffer commercial harm from state-licensed marijuana operators now competing under the same Schedule III classification without equivalent safety review. Supporting the stay motion, Harvard Medical School neuroscientist Dr. Bertha K. Madras filed an expert declaration (also June 9) warning the D.C. Circuit that rescheduling poses 'substantial' and 'unacceptably high' public health risks — particularly for adolescents and unborn children — and that marijuana does not meet the standards required of a medicine. This is a distinct stay motion from the June 4 SAM/NDASA opening brief. Petitioners may also seek emergency relief before the June 29 broader-rescheduling ALJ hearing. No court ruling has issued as of June 19, 2026.
items.whyItMatters: This is the first formal motion in Case 26-1136 asking the D.C. Circuit to actually halt the order. A granted stay would revert state medical marijuana to Schedule I, nullify all DEA registrations filed under the expedited pathway, and undo 280E relief. Oklahoma operators filing DEA registration before the June 26–27 window preserves the safe-harbor regardless of litigation outcome; the risk of not registering (OBNDD sanctions, license jeopardy) is immediate and certain, while stay risk is real but not yet realized.

items.headline: Broader-Rescheduling ALJ Hearing Set for June 29 – July 15, 2026 — Only Rescheduling Opponents Selected as Participants; Constitutional Challenge Active
items.summary: Alongside the partial rescheduling, DEA withdrew its stalled August 2024 proceeding and issued a new Notice of Hearing for an expedited ALJ proceeding on whether ALL marijuana — including adult-use — should move to Schedule III via notice-and-comment rulemaking. The hearing runs June 29 – July 15, 2026 (July 3 recess) at DEA's Arlington, VA facility. PARTICIPANT SELECTION (June 18–19): DEA released its participant list and ALL 7 selected parties oppose rescheduling: National Drug & Alcohol Screening Association (NDASA); Tennessee Bureau of Investigation; Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM); the states of Nebraska, Idaho, Indiana, and Louisiana; DUID Victim Voices; Kenneth Finn, MD; and Phillip A. Drum, PharmD. NORML and all cannabis industry, patient, and reform organizations were excluded — zero pro-reform parties selected. A pre-hearing constitutional challenge is also active: the DOJ formally admitted in MMJ BioPharma Cultivation Inc. v. Bondi (Feb. 27, 2025) that DEA ALJ removal protections are unconstitutional; challengers argue that under Axon v. FTC (2022), subjecting parties to proceedings before an unlawful tribunal is itself irreparable injury. MMJ International announced plans to seek emergency injunctive relief against the hearing. If MMJ files an emergency motion against the hearing, the D.C. Circuit could be forced to rule on the constitutional question within days. No injunction has been granted and the hearing remains on schedule as of June 19, 2026.
items.whyItMatters: The hearing's all-opponent participant roster means the administrative record will be built exclusively by rescheduling opponents — no commercial, patient, or consumer perspective included. This structural imbalance may strengthen D.C. Circuit petitioners' procedural arguments and increases the risk that the broader rescheduling recommendation will oppose Schedule III for adult-use marijuana. For Oklahoma operators, neither the hearing's outcome nor its participant composition affects the April 28 state-medical-marijuana Schedule III order already in effect, nor does it change the June 26–27 registration deadline.

items.headline: Chief ALJ Derek Julius Signs Scheduling Order — June 29 Hearing Explicitly Limited to Adult-Use 'Remainder'; State Medical Marijuana Already Done; Prehearing Deadlines June 24
items.summary: DEA Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius signed a 12-page scheduling order on June 19, 2026, setting the procedural roadmap for the June 29–July 15 broader-rescheduling hearing. Key provisions: (1) government attorneys must file notices of appearance by June 22; (2) designated parties must file prehearing statements (≤25 pages each) by June 24; (3) parties must exchange proposed exhibits by June 24–25; (4) the ALJ will issue a detailed hearing schedule by June 24; (5) the hearing recesses July 3 and reconvenes July 6. CRITICAL SCOPE CLARIFICATION: The order explicitly states 'the scope of this hearing is not to discuss the rescheduling of medical products approved by the Food and Drug Administration that contain marijuana and of medical marijuana products already regulated by the states, which has already occurred' and that 'the narrow issue in this matter is whether the remainder of marijuana, as defined in the CSA, should be transferred from its current place on schedule I of the list of controlled substances to schedule III.' The government carries the burden of proof as proponent of the rule.
items.whyItMatters: The ALJ's explicit scope language provides official confirmation that the June 29 hearing does not threaten the April 28 Schedule III status of Oklahoma state-licensed medical marijuana operators — that rescheduling is already done and is not at issue in the administrative proceeding. The hearing determines only whether adult-use/recreational marijuana also moves to Schedule III. For OMMA-licensed cultivators and dispensaries, this means the DEA registration obligation, 280E exemption, and all compliance burdens from the April 28 order are NOT on the line at this hearing. D.C. Circuit litigation remains a separate and real risk. Oklahoma operators' immediate priority remains filing DEA registration — dispensary portal CLOSED June 22; cultivators/manufacturers must use Form 225 before June 26–27 (2 days remaining as of June 24).

source.name: Marijuana Moment — DEA Judge Issues Order Laying Out Process For Hearing This Month

items.headline: NORML Files Emergency Reconsideration After DEA Excludes All Pro-Reform Groups from June 29 ALJ Hearing
items.summary: Following the DEA's release of the June 29 hearing participant list — which includes only rescheduling opponents — NORML filed an emergency request for reconsideration with the DEA on approximately June 20, 2026, arguing that excluding all pro-reform parties from the broader-rescheduling ALJ hearing violates the public interest. NORML contended that the exclusion 'would cause immediate and irreparable procedural prejudice, impair the completeness and balance of the administrative record, and disserve the public interest in a full and reasoned proceeding concerning the federal legal status of marijuana.' The American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp (ATACH) — also excluded — called the selection 'deeply disappointing' and stated it would continue advocacy through the Coalition for Cannabis Scheduling Reform. The DEA had already issued formal participant notifications on June 22; as of June 23, 2026, no public DEA response to NORML's reconsideration has been issued and the June 29 hearing remains on schedule with only the seven anti-rescheduling participants.
items.whyItMatters: NORML's emergency reconsideration confirms that the all-opponent participant roster is being formally challenged through administrative channels, not just commentary. If the DEA denies reconsideration — the likely outcome given notifications already issued — NORML and excluded industry groups may escalate to the D.C. Circuit, adding new procedural claims to the consolidated rescheduling challenges (26-1106/1130/1136). For Oklahoma operators, this does NOT affect the already-effective Schedule III status for state-licensed medical marijuana (Chief ALJ Julius's June 19 order explicitly excludes that from the hearing's scope). The June 29 hearing and its one-sided record remain a risk factor for the future of broader adult-use rescheduling only. Oklahoma operators' immediate priority remains filing DEA registration via Form 225 before June 26–27 — 2 days remain as of June 24.

items.headline: 280E Tax Deduction Bar Lifted for Medical Operators — Binding IRS/Treasury Guidance Still Pending
items.summary: State-licensed medical marijuana is no longer Schedule I/II, so operators are no longer subject to the IRC Section 280E deduction disallowance. Treasury/IRS announced April 23, 2026 that formal guidance is forthcoming and expected to treat rescheduling as applying for the full 2026 tax year. As of June 19, 2026 — over seven weeks after the order took effect — no revenue ruling, IRS notice, proposed regulation, or other binding written guidance has been published. Seven House Democrats formally demanded IRS and Treasury expedite guidance on May 28 (see companion item). No retroactive relief for prior years has been announced; recreational-only operators remain fully subject to 280E.
items.whyItMatters: Potentially tens of millions in aggregate annual tax savings for medical operators; however, operators and CPAs are acting on legal interpretation alone until IRS publishes binding guidance. Allocation methodologies for mixed-use operators and retroactivity scope remain unresolved. A May 2026 DOJ lawsuit demanding return of a cannabis MSO's pre-rescheduling 280E refund signals IRS will aggressively contest any pre-2026 retroactive claims.

source.name: U.S. Treasury

items.headline: IRS/Treasury 280E Guidance Still Not Issued — Seven House Democrats Demand Action
items.summary: Seven House Democrats led by Reps. Steven Horsford and Steve Cohen wrote to IRS Commissioner Danny Bisignano and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on May 28, 2026, demanding prompt publication of formal 280E guidance following the April 28 medical-marijuana rescheduling order. As of June 19, 2026 — over seven weeks after rescheduling took effect — neither IRS nor Treasury has published a revenue ruling, IRS notice, proposed regulation, or other binding written guidance on how 280E applies to Schedule III medical-marijuana operators. The April 23 Treasury press release (SB0471) announced intent to issue guidance including a transition rule treating relief as applying for the full 2026 taxable year; it is not itself binding. Operators and CPAs are acting on the legal interpretation that 280E does not apply to state-licensed medical activity, but without IRS confirmation of allocation methodologies or treatment of mixed-use operators.
items.whyItMatters: Oklahoma medical-marijuana operators — cultivators, processors, and dispensaries — cannot finalize 2026 tax strategy with certainty until IRS publishes formal guidance. The seven-week gap between the rescheduling order and any binding IRS action leaves operators exposed if Treasury ultimately limits relief in ways not currently anticipated.

secondarySource.name: The Marijuana Herald — Lawmakers Urge IRS and Treasury

items.headline: DOJ Sues TerrAscend for $8.3M in First Known 280E Refund Clawback — IRS Signals Pre-2026 Claims Will Be Contested
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice filed suit May 18, 2026 in U.S. District Court in New Jersey seeking $8.3 million plus interest from cannabis MSO TerrAscend USA — the first known instance of the federal government attempting to recover a 280E tax refund proactively claimed by a cannabis operator. TerrAscend filed an amended 2020 tax return in April 2024 claiming $64.2 million in deductions not permitted under Section 280E, and the IRS sent an $8.3M refund check in June 2024. The DOJ complaint alleges the refund was 'erroneous' because IRS's Joint Committee on Taxation did not review it as required and because TerrAscend was not entitled to the deductions. An IRS bulletin issued the same month TerrAscend received the refund had already warned that amended returns seeking 280E relief were 'not entitled to a refund or payment.' TerrAscend deposited the check the same day it arrived and has 'not voluntarily returned' the funds. Across publicly traded cannabis MSOs, total disputed 280E claims total approximately $1.6 billion.
items.whyItMatters: IRS and DOJ have drawn a clear line: pre-rescheduling 280E refund claims for tax years before 2026 will be aggressively contested, not honored. Oklahoma dispensaries and cultivators considering amended returns for 2024, 2023, or earlier years face the same enforcement risk. The April 28 rescheduling order eliminates 280E going forward (January 1, 2026 and after, per expected Treasury guidance), but IRS has signaled it will fight retroactive relief for prior years without formal written authorization — which has still not been published as of June 19, 2026. Do NOT file pre-2026 amended returns without specialized tax counsel.

items.headline: Congress Closes the Hemp Loophole — Delta-8 / THCA / Synthetics Banned Effective Nov 12, 2026
items.summary: The Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (H.R. 5371 §781), enacted November 12, 2025, rewrote the federal hemp definition: the 0.3% THC threshold now counts total THC including THCA; final consumable products are capped at 0.4 mg total THC per container; intermediates are capped at 0.3% total THC dry-weight post-decarboxylation; cannabinoids not naturally produced by the plant or synthesized outside it are excluded and treated as Schedule I. Products exceeding thresholds after November 12, 2026 revert to Schedule I.
items.whyItMatters: Functionally eliminates the current Delta-8/Delta-10/THCA-flower intoxicating-hemp market unless reformulated or Congress acts before the effective date.

source.name: Arnold & Porter Advisory

items.headline: Oklahoma Grower License: Current Compliance Stack — Metrc, OBNDD Registration, 75% Residency, $50K Bond
items.summary: Commercial growers must comply with OMMA rules and hold an OBNDD "Manufacturer" registration. Tier-1 fees range $2,558.30 to $50,000+ by canopy size.

items.headline: OMMA New Testing Laboratory Rules Take Effect June 1, 2026
items.summary: OMMA's updated permanent testing laboratory rules took effect June 1, 2026, the product of a multi-year process directed by HB 4056 (2022) in which seven licensed lab directors met across 15 sessions (90+ hours) and submitted 120 pages of recommendations. The rules amend OAC 442:10-8-1 and OAC 442:10-8-3 and address manufacturer's instructions for use, enrichment steps and quality control sample requirements, inventory tag requirements, and clarifications on yeast/mold and potency-confirmation testing for distillate. A prior set of emergency rule updates for licensed laboratories was approved separately. Stakeholders at the public comment hearing had pressed OMMA for clearer standards and broader lab access to Metrc data.
items.whyItMatters: Cultivators and processors submitting products for third-party testing must now meet the updated standards. Products that fail under new methodology cannot legally enter the distribution chain. Labs out of compliance with the new equipment or procedural rules face potential OMMA enforcement, which could create bottlenecks affecting product release timelines for growers and manufacturers.

items.headline: Oklahoma Cannabis Market in Freefall — Wholesale Prices Down 63%, 6,000+ Grows Shuttered
items.summary: Oklahoma Watch and KGOU (NPR Oklahoma) reported June 2, 2026 that the state's medical cannabis market is in severe contraction. Wholesale prices have fallen from approximately $3,000/lb at peak to $1,100/lb (≈63% decline), making Oklahoma the national price floor at $2.11/gram. A 2023 study found licensed supply exceeded patient demand by roughly 64 to 1. At peak, Oklahoma had nearly 14,000 licensed businesses including ~9,400 growers; more than 6,000 grow locations have since shut down or been abandoned. The industry generated $670M+ in retail sales and $1.1B+ in wholesale transactions in 2025, contributing ~$47M in excise taxes and $60M+ in state and local sales taxes — but revenue and margins are collapsing. Governor Stitt is calling for voters to shut the program down entirely; legislative leadership has resisted abolition.
items.whyItMatters: Oklahoma cultivators and processors face existential margin pressure from oversupply and falling wholesale prices at the same moment new DEA registration costs ($3,699/yr for manufacturers) are being imposed. Dispensary customers face the same squeeze from the retail side. The license moratorium extension (HB 3143, signed May 2026) prevents new entrants but does nothing to reduce the existing licensed supply overhang. CAKE and its wholesale dispensary customers operate in this environment — the cost and compliance burden of DEA registration compounds an already-stressed market.

items.headline: DEA Begins On-Site Inspections at Cannabis Businesses That Registered Under Schedule III
items.summary: The Drug Enforcement Administration began conducting on-site inspections at state-licensed cannabis businesses that applied for federal DEA registration following the April 28 rescheduling order. The Mississippi Medical Marijuana Association reported that two of its dispensary members were among the first in the country visited after submitting applications through the DEA Medical Marijuana Dispensary Registration Portal. High Street Dispensary in Jackson, MS (owner David Fowler) hosted 5–6 DEA representatives for approximately six hours; Fowler described the agents as 'very cordial' and 'did not come in overbearing,' noting the agents said they were 'new to this whole process too' and approached the visit as collaborative and inquisitive. Both visited dispensaries were told they were among the first in the country to receive inspections. DEA inspections are a standard step in processing new Schedule III registration applications — agents verify facility compliance, security, records, and personnel information provided in the application.
items.whyItMatters: This is the first confirmed ground-level evidence that DEA's Schedule III oversight is now operational — registration is not a paper exercise but triggers physical federal presence at the facility. Oklahoma dispensaries and cultivators/manufacturers who file registration applications (dispensary portal by June 22; Form 225 by June 26–27) should expect an in-person DEA visit as part of the review process. Before filing, operators must ensure their facilities, employee documentation (SSNs for all personnel with controlled-substance access), security systems, record-keeping, and chain-of-custody logs are in order. The collaborative tone at these first visits is consistent with DEA's standard registration process — Schedule III inspections under 21 U.S.C. 880 include authority to enter at any time without advance notice. The inspection news does not change OBNDD's mandatory registration directive for manufacturers and distributors; it does mean non-registration avoidance strategies based on 'avoiding DEA visibility' are now tested against reality.

items.headline: Oklahoma HB 4454 Signed — Edibles Restricted to 10mg/Serving, 100mg/Package; Cartoon Shapes and Minor-Targeted Marketing Banned; Effective November 1, 2026

Products in licensed inventory after November 1 that exceed the per-serving or per-package THC caps, or feature banned shapes, are out of compliance. Given OMMA's active enforcement posture (6,000+ inspections, 704 products recalled), this is an enforcement-ready standard. items.headline: Rohrabacher-Blumenauer Rider Expired July 2025 — RESTORED by P.L. 119-74 (Signed January 23, 2026); Anti-Rescheduling Block Excluded from Final Appropriations
items.summary: The Rohrabacher-Blumenauer rider (also known as the Joyce-Leahy amendment) — which since FY2015 had prohibited the DOJ from spending appropriated funds to interfere with individuals acting in compliance with state medical marijuana laws — was excluded from the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' signed July 4, 2025. Since that date, DOJ has no appropriations-based prohibition on prosecuting state-legal medical cannabis operators under the CSA. This removes the practical backstop that had protected OMMA-compliant operators from federal prosecution even without a federal registration. UPDATE (P.L. 119-74, SIGNED JANUARY 23, 2026): The FY2026 Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies Appropriations Act (P.L. 119-74) restored the medical marijuana state protections rider via Section 531, ending the ~6.5-month gap (July 4, 2025 – January 23, 2026). Oklahoma is covered; Idaho, Kansas, Nebraska, and American Samoa are explicitly excluded. The House Appropriations version of Section 607 that would have blocked DEA from rescheduling cannabis was removed from the final bicameral agreement.
items.whyItMatters: UPDATED — RIDER RESTORED: The rider was absent July 4, 2025 – January 23, 2026 (~6.5 months). Since P.L. 119-74 was signed January 23, 2026, Oklahoma OMMA-licensed operators again have Congressional appropriations-based protection: DOJ cannot use appropriated funds to target OMMA-compliant operators for activities lawful under Oklahoma medical marijuana law. However, this does not replace DEA registration: (1) the rider bars DOJ enforcement spending but does not grant positive federal compliance authority or registration status; (2) the OBNDD mandatory DEA registration obligation (enforcement from January 1, 2027) is independently imposed by Oklahoma state law; (3) the rider provides no 280E tax relief; (4) if the April 28 rescheduling order is stayed or vacated by the D.C. Circuit, the rider's medical marijuana state protections would still apply independently as a separate protection layer. The exclusion of Section 607 (rescheduling block) from P.L. 119-74 means Congress has affirmatively declined to block the April 28 rescheduling order through the appropriations process.

items.headline: ALJ Hearing Day 2 (June 30): Opponents Attack Government's CAMU Methodology — Five-to-Two-Part Test Switch Introduced 2 Months Before FDA Finished Analysis; Burchman Testifies Marijuana Replaced Opioids for Pain Patients
items.summary: On the second day of the broader-rescheduling ALJ hearing (June 30, 2026), two developments shaped the administrative record. First, Dr. Corey Burchman — a New Hampshire board-certified anesthesiologist and pain management physician who practiced until 2019 — testified that once medical cannabis became available at Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center, he and colleagues would 'avidly use that ability to limit opioids,' with some patients fully transitioning off prescription painkillers. He called cannabis 'extremely helpful in chronic pain patients as a means of analgesia.' Second, and more legally consequential: opponents cross-examined FDA's Dominic Chiapperino about the government's switch from a prior five-part test to a new two-part test for determining 'currently accepted medical use' (CAMU) — the CAMU determination is the legal keystone that classifies marijuana as Schedule III rather than Schedule I. An attorney for the states of Idaho, Indiana, and Nebraska pressed Chiapperino about a 2015 FDA analysis that concluded marijuana did not have CAMU, noting the new two-part test did not exist when that analysis began. Chiapperino acknowledged the new two-part test was introduced in July 2023 — just two months before FDA analysts finished the current analysis. The DOJ's OLC determined in 2024 that the prior five-part test was 'impermissibly narrow,' but opponents argued the midstream methodology change was improper. The government's ALJ attorney said the hearing was not the forum to litigate that dispute. The seven anti-rescheduling hearing participants all had the right to cross-examine the government's witnesses.
items.whyItMatters: The two-part CAMU test controversy is the opponents' sharpest line of attack — it challenges not the policy outcome but the legal methodology used to reach it, which is the kind of procedural argument federal courts evaluate under APA 'arbitrary and capricious' review. If the D.C. Circuit concludes the government improperly changed its CAMU methodology mid-analysis, it could vacate or stay the April 28 Schedule III order. Oklahoma OMMA operators' immediate compliance posture is unchanged: window closed June 29; operators who filed hold safe-harbor; those who did not should apply now via Form 225 at deadiversion.usdoj.gov; OBNDD enforcement begins January 1, 2027. However, compliance directors should monitor the DOJ's July 2 D.C. Circuit response brief for how the government defends the two-part CAMU test switch — this will signal the litigation strength of the April 28 order going forward.

items.headline: DOJ Files D.C. Circuit Response Brief July 2 — Challengers 'Come Nowhere Near' Stay Standard; 'Pocketbook Interests' Attack on NDASA/MMJ Standing
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice filed its response brief in consolidated D.C. Circuit rescheduling challenges (Cases 26-1106/1130/1136) on July 2, 2026, opposing petitioners' stay and vacatur motions. Three key legal arguments: (1) STAY STANDARD — Challengers 'come nowhere near' meeting the four-factor standard required for a stay. (2) STANDING — DOJ argued NDASA failed to establish Article III standing, offering only 'generalized speculation about how the rescheduling order might affect the drug-testing industry rather than particularized allegations about how the order has affected specific members of the association.' (3) ZONE OF INTERESTS — DOJ argued petitioners' alleged injuries fall outside the CSA's purpose: Congress enacted the law to protect public health and ensure proper regulation for medical/scientific purposes, 'not to guarantee revenue for drug screeners or protect future market opportunities for cannabinoid-based pharmaceuticals.' DOJ characterized petitioners as invoking 'pocketbook interests served by keeping all marijuana in schedule I.' The D.C. Circuit can now rule on the stay motion at any time following this brief.
items.whyItMatters: The DOJ brief is the government's substantive legal defense of the April 28 Schedule III order in the D.C. Circuit — the forum where the most consequential risk to Oklahoma operators lies. The strong stay-standard framing ('nowhere near'), standing challenge, and 'pocketbook interests' characterization collectively represent a comprehensive government defense of the order.
